Condition: MID

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
Every twenty years, at Ise, they tear down the shrine and build it again.

Not renovate. Not repair. They clear an adjacent plot of white gravel, fell fresh cypress, and raise the buildings from nothing—the same joinery, the same thatched roofs, the same proportions arrived at sometime in the seventh century. Then they dismantle the old one. The cycle has run, with a long lapse during the warring states period, for something like thirteen hundred years. The most sacred wooden structure in Japan is never more than two decades old.

This confuses the Western category of "oldest building," and I think the confusion is the point. What Ise preserves is not wood. Wood is the least durable part of the operation. What it preserves is a body of knowledge dense enough to survive the death of everyone who holds it: how to select a tree, how to read grain, how to cut a joint that will hold through a typhoon season without a single nail. The Ship of Theseus stops being a paradox once you notice that the ship was never the planks. The ship was the shipwright's hands, and the planks are just what those hands do.

The twenty-year interval is not arbitrary. It's roughly a human career divided into three. A carpenter comes to the first rebuilding as an apprentice who mostly watches and carries things. He comes to the second as a master who does the difficult work. He comes to the third as an old man who stands at the edge and says *no, like this*. Three cycles, sixty years, and the knowledge has been passed through two full handoffs without ever being written down in a way that would matter. You could photograph every joint at Ise and still not be able to build it. The archive is not sufficient. The archive has never been sufficient. The thing only lives in the interval between one pair of hands and the next, and if that interval stretches too long, it dies quietly, and nobody notices until someone tries to use it.

I find myself thinking about this more than is probably normal.

We are a species that tells stories about creation and almost none about upkeep. Genesis is a building story. Every founding myth is a building story. We name buildings after the people who paid for them and occasionally after the people who designed them, and essentially never after the person who kept the roof from leaking for forty years. There is no monument anywhere to a janitor. Meanwhile the actual proportion of human effort that goes into keeping things working, versus bringing new things into existence, is something like a hundred to one, and the ratio is invisible because of a cruel structural fact: maintenance is only perceptible when it fails.

Done perfectly, it looks like nothing happening. The bridge that doesn't collapse. The sewer that doesn't back up. The anesthesiologist whose patient simply wakes up. There's an entire category of human excellence whose signature is the absence of an event, which means it can't be photographed, can't be narrated, and can't be defended in a budget meeting except by counterfactual, and counterfactuals are the weakest currency there is. Every maintenance department in the world is arguing with ghosts. *Here is the disaster that did not occur.* Nobody has ever won that argument cleanly.

Software people learned this the hard way, having assumed for a while that they'd escaped it. Code doesn't wear out. Bits don't rust. And yet software rots anyway, because the world moves underneath it—the compiler changes, the dependency is abandoned, the protocol deprecates, the certificate expires. A program is not an object; it's a standing agreement with an environment, and environments do not hold still. For years OpenSSL sat underneath a large fraction of the encrypted internet, maintained by a handful of people on donations amounting to roughly nothing, until Heartbleed made the arrangement briefly visible to everyone, after which it stopped being visible again. More recently, a backdoor was slipped into a compression library by someone who spent *years* patiently befriending an exhausted solo maintainer, and who understood, correctly, that the softest target in the entire supply chain was a tired man being told he wasn't doing enough. That is an attack on upkeep itself. It's the most modern crime I can think of.

Underneath all of it is thermodynamics, which is not sentimental. Order is expensive and disorder is free. A house is a slow argument with weather, and weather has infinite patience and no other obligations. The moment you stop arguing, you don't get a grace period; the water is already in the joint. Everything that exists is being actively held out of equilibrium, and the holding is the thing, and the object is just the residue of the holding. Ise is honest about this in a way almost nothing else is. It doesn't pretend the building persists. It admits the building is a verb and builds the verb into the calendar.

I suspect the same is true of most things I'd actually care about. Friendship, for instance, seems badly described by the language of construction—we speak of *building* relationships, *foundations*, *bonds*, as if there were a moment of completion after which the structure stood on its own. But nobody has ever had a friend the way they have a bookshelf. What you have is a practice of attention that either continues or doesn't, and the friendship is the name for the continuing. The people I'd imagine as having long marriages don't describe an achievement. They describe a maintenance schedule so thoroughly internalized it stopped feeling like one: the coffee, the walk, the same three arguments handled gently for thirty years, the small daily re-thatching that keeps the rain out.

At Ise, next to the standing shrine, there is always an empty lot. White pebbles, raked, and a small hut in the center sheltering a wooden post. It looks like nothing. It's the most important part of the site: it's the twenty years of waiting made physical, the space held open for the next set of hands. They're growing the cypress for it now, trees planted by people who knew they'd be dead before the felling. The building is twenty years old and thirteen hundred. Both are true. The gravel is not empty. It's full of the only thing that actually lasts, which is somebody's decision to do it again.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, argument-driven reflection turns the rebuilding of Ise into a meditation on maintenance, transmitted skill, and care.

## Grounded reading
The voice is assured and essayistic, but it keeps interrupting its broad claims with personal attention: “I find myself thinking about this more than is probably normal,” then later, “I suspect the same is true of most things I'd actually care about.” Its pathos lies in what goes unnoticed: the worker whose skill prevents disaster, the friendship kept alive by ordinary attention, the trees planted by people who will not see them felled. The reader is invited to reconsider preservation not as keeping an object unchanged, but as sustaining the practice that lets it continue.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds Ise’s empty lot, the passing of craft between generations, invisible maintenance, software vulnerabilities, thermodynamic decay, and friendship. It repeatedly makes care and continuity visible through concrete images—the joint that holds, the roof kept from leaking, the coffee and walk, the cypress growing for a future rebuilding—and gives them greater moral weight than creation or monument-making.

## Evidence line
> I find myself thinking about this more than is probably normal.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample’s distinctive metaphors and sustained return to upkeep make its chosen emphasis unusually clear and coherent.
